results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

Every outliner summary matches the controlling idea of the spec paragraph it is aligned to, in the spec's order (p01, p02, p04, p03, then p05 through p42 as declared, including stages after reading and in-practice after when-it-goes-wrong); the three callouts carry the roadmap, thesis statement and failure-pattern banner and match no paragraph.

The four units the outliner flagged hold one controlling idea each: Introduction ¶1 is a funnel from the store-pickup hook to the thesis the spec places there (p01); 'What a Capability Is' ¶3 announces 'Two more terms' and defines both as the map's boxes and arrows (p11); 'Typical Flows' ¶2 opens 'Two patterns stand out' read from one table (p19); 'Three Ways' ¶5 opens 'Two variants are worth naming' (p25). Each pair sits under one announced umbrella, as the spec declares.

Every body paragraph ties to a supporting claim through its section: scene and capability to S1, map to S2, flows to S3, three ways to S4, reading to S6, stages to S5, failures to S5/S6, in-practice to S1/S6; introduction and conclusion units frame or synthesize the thesis.

results.draft_locus: Three Ways to Cover the Map ¶2
results.quote: Adobe's October 2026 information center lists three deployment options for Adobe Commerce (on-premises, on Adobe's cloud infrastructure, or as a fully managed cloud service).
results.finding: The three deployment options are given right after the claim 'Even a suite vendor sells a part meant to sit beside someone else's product' but do not show it and no sentence says what they show; only the Commerce Optimizer sentence supports the claim. Both flow readers stopped here (A12, B11). Say what the deployment options show or lead with Commerce Optimizer so the claim lands on its evidence.

results.draft_locus: In Practice: Kestrel & Pine's Systems on the Map ¶1
results.quote: 62% of wholesale orders; 38% keyed into the ERP by hand
results.finding: Every other row of the table gives a status on the map (empty, overlap, covered); this row gives two percentages without saying what they mean on the map (the B2B box is only partly covered, the rest an unowned manual flow into the ERP). Flow reader B had to infer it (B17).

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶3
results.quote: **Where we are in the order's journey.** Eva's jacket passes through search, pricing, checkout, delivery and possibly a return.
results.finding: Declared: example, carrying over capabilities, the systems that handle them and the handoffs between them. The paragraph opens on a series signpost and on Eva's jacket without tying it to the requests and unowned handoffs of ¶2, so it reads as an interruption between the three questions and the roadmap (both flow readers, A2 and B3) rather than as an example of them.

results.draft_locus: Introduction ¶1

A short gloss of 'business fact' and 'home' in place keeps the spec's order.

The introduction opens on an intriguing example (the store-pickup request) and states a specific thesis; it is none of the five weak patterns.

The conclusion opens with the callback, synthesizes, sorts its points by how settled they are, ends with questions and a hand-off; the evidence it names recalls the body's rather than introducing new evidence, and no new subtopic appears.

'What to Take Away' ¶1 states what no single section states (one home per fact, every other holder a copy fed by a flow, a product a claim on boxes that leaves the flows to the merchant) and says why it matters: the places a landscape will fail show on the map before the business; the synthesis bullets add the three marks and the joins nobody can buy.

The conclusion opens on the store-pickup request and places it on the map: cart and checkout, inventory and availability, store operations and the flows between them, with a pickup app claiming one box at most, as callback.how asks.

From the introduction alone the reader predicted every roadmap section in order (hook, whiteboard, definitions, map, flows, three ways and product-page reading, stages, four failures, Kestrel & Pine on the map), the kind of evidence (the running fictional case, Eva's jacket, vendors' public pages) and the plain teaching tone.

Reader placed the claim on order management (holding every order and steering it to fulfillment) and named the neighbouring capabilities left out: inventory and availability, and warehouse and fulfillment (physical stock, picking), matching the expected 'not warehouse management or inventory counting'.

Reader said every system looks complete from the inside so a list hides gaps and overlaps, and to draw the capabilities first and place systems in them: an overlap as one box with several names, a gap as an empty box.

Reader named it a derived fact (available-to-promise), computed from stock on hand minus commitments to unshipped orders minus a buffer, owned by the calculation, and said a hand edit bypasses it and can make the storefront promise what the warehouse cannot deliver.
Reader named prices, orders and payments as exact in near real time, and said the others tolerate lag with a reconciliation behind them, finance as a daily batch.

Reader stated the rule (cover the center with one product you do not customize, operations with products built for operations, own the joins) and that the joins stay with the merchant whichever vendor it picks.
